validation.title: 2. Experimental Validation
validation.intro: The two workflows below replay published electroporation experiments using this platform's physics models. Each workflow loads the exact cell parameters, field settings, and protocol steps from the cited paper, runs the simulation, and reports how closely the computed outcome matches the published result. A scientist can reproduce these in under two minutes to verify the model before designing their own protocol.

overview.title: 1. Overview

capGrid.area: Closed-loop σᵢ calibration and residual tiers

overview.p1: ResoPulse is a research simulation platform for studying frequency-selective electrostimulation of biological membranes, the question of whether an applied electric field can preferentially disrupt target cells (cancer, bacteria, or viruses) while leaving healthy tissue below the damage threshold. Uniquely, ResoPulse is a closed-loop digital twin: every measured outcome you log (target/healthy lysis, viability, PI+, qPCR, temperature) feeds a calibration cycle that fits a per-cell σᵢ multiplier, scores residuals tier-by-tier, and drives active-learning suggestions for the next experiment. The central predictive metric is the Selectivity Index (TI): the ratio of healthy-to-target lysis field. The platform computes the transmembrane potential (Vm) induced by a uniform alternating electric field using the Schwan single-shell dielectric model (Kotnik & Miklavcic [9]), the specific absorption rate (SAR) and steady-state temperature via the Pennes bioheat equation [16], and the disruption ratio for each cell type. Advanced controls include field-to-cell orientation (cos θ), blood perfusion rate (ωb), cell packing fraction (φ), and Maxwell-Garnett effective medium correction for dense suspensions.
overview.p2: Two operating modes are available via the mode toggle: (1) Schwan / IRE, cancer vs. healthy mammalian cell targeting via transmembrane potential (100-10,000 V/cm, DC to ~10 MHz); (2) Acoustic Resonance, bacterial cell-wall or viral capsid disruption via mechanical resonance of the protein shell or peptidoglycan layer (modelled 0.1-50 GHz, unvalidated at RF). A third sub-threshold state, Sub-threshold Biomodulation, is computed automatically within IRE mode when the healthy cell disruption ratio is in the 8-45% range: PIEZO1 Ca²⁺ and NO signalling (sub-lytic nourishing window, see §2.10). This is not a separate mode, it is a state detected by the same Schwan model at reduced field intensity. Each cell type has a characteristic frequency fc = 1/(2πτ) set by its radius and membrane capacitance; selectivity is maximised at frequencies where target and healthy cells respond differently. Scope note: Tumour Treating Fields (TTFields, Kirson et al. [2]) operate at ~1-3 V/cm and 100-300 kHz via dielectrophoretic forces on the mitotic spindle, a sub-threshold non-Vm mechanism outside the scope of this model. This platform models the IRE/electroporation regime (≥100 V/cm threshold crossing).
overview.disclaimer: This platform is intended for research visualisation only and does not constitute clinical guidance or a validated medical device. All biophysical parameters are approximate values derived from the bioelectromagnetics literature. Every computed value is a model prediction, not a measured quantity. Known approximations and model limitations are documented in each section of the Physical Model chapter.
overview.honesty: Simulation transparency: ResoPulse computes model predictions from published biophysical equations. No value displayed in this platform is a measured laboratory result. All physics models involve simplifying assumptions that are documented in the corresponding section (§3.1-3.13). Where a model uses empirical constants, population-averaged values, or unvalidated extrapolations, this is stated explicitly. If you observe a discrepancy between a simulated value and a measured result from your own experiment, use the Discrepancy Report link at the top of this page.

schwan.title: 3.1 Schwan Equation
schwan.tip: Schwan Single-Shell Model Predicts peak transmembrane voltage Vm(f) = 1.5·E·R·cosθ / √(1+(ωτ)²) τ = R·Cm·(2σe+σi)/(2σe·σi) · Cm = εr·ε₀/d · fc = 1/(2πτ) At quasi-DC (f≪fc): Vm ≈ 1.5·E·R · Selectivity = R_T / R_H Above fc: Vm falls -20 dB/decade (larger cells roll off first).
schwan.p1: For a spherical cell modelled as a single-shell dielectric in a uniform AC electric field, the peak induced transmembrane potential is given by the Schwan equation. The cos θ factor accounts for the angle between the applied field and the cell's long axis: θ = 0° (field-aligned) yields maximum coupling; θ = 90° gives Vm = 0. Crucially, cos θ cancels exactly in the selectivity ratio Vm,T/Vm,H, so field orientation does not affect the Selectivity Index (TI), it scales both cells equally. The orientation slider in the Advanced panel rotates both cells simultaneously.
schwan.p2: The membrane time constant τ determines the characteristic frequency f<sub>c</sub> = 1/(2πτ), above which V<sub>m</sub> falls at −20 dB/decade. Cells with large radius R, high membrane permittivity ε<sub>r</sub>, or thin membrane d exhibit a larger C<sub>m</sub> and lower f<sub>c</sub>, making them preferentially disrupted at lower frequencies relative to smaller reference cells. The extracellular conductivity σ<sub>e</sub> is temperature-corrected at each simulation step using a medium-specific coefficient α: σ<sub>e</sub>(T) = σ<sub>e0</sub> × (1 + α × (T − 37°C)), which shifts τ and f<sub>c</sub> dynamically as the medium heats. α is 0.020/°C for saline, DMEM, PBS, RPMI, and EP buffer; 0.017/°C for whole blood; 0.015/°C for soft tissue; 0.028/°C for distilled water (Gabriel et al. [21]; Foster & Schwan [5]).
schwan.eqSub1: ω = 2πf    τ = R · C<sub>m</sub> · (2σ<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>i</sub>) / (2σ<sub>e</sub> · σ<sub>i</sub>)
schwan.eqSub3: cos θ = |cos(θ)|, field-to-cell-axis coupling factor; θ = 0° (field-aligned) → max V<sub>m</sub>; θ = 60° default = <|cos θ|> = 0.5 for isotropic 3D suspension; cancels in V<sub>m,T</sub>/V<sub>m,H</sub> selectivity ratio; σ<sub>e</sub>(T) = σ<sub>e0</sub>·(1 + α·(T−37°C)) where α is medium-specific: 0.020/°C saline, 0.017/°C blood, 0.015/°C tissue, 0.028/°C water (see §2.2 for full list)
schwan.eqNote: Tadej Kotnik & Damijan Miklavcic, Biophys. J. 79:670 (2000) [9]

thermal.title: 3.2 SAR & Pennes Bioheat Model
thermal.tip: SAR and Pennes Bioheat SAR = σi · α² · E² · wf / ρ [W/kg] α = 3σe/(2σe+σi) · wf = 0.5 (CW sinusoidal) or 1.0 (pulsed) T_ss = 37 + SAR·dc / (λ·cp) · λ = 0.02 s⁻¹ Newton cooling Blood perfusion: λ_perf = ωb × 63.9 / cp (Pennes 1948)
thermal.p1: Ohmic heating is modelled via the specific absorption rate (SAR). The internal field factor α = 3σ<sub>e</sub>/(2σ<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>i</sub>) is the exact DC Clausius-Mossotti solution for a conducting sphere in a uniform field (Foster & Schwan [5]). At frequencies above f<sub>c</sub>, the membrane capacitance shields the cell interior, so the displayed SAR is an upper bound that grows as f → f<sub>c</sub> from below.
thermal.p2: Steady-state temperature follows the Pennes bioheat equation [16] with two parallel cooling pathways: Newton surface cooling (λNewton = 0.02 s⁻¹, representing combined thermal diffusion and surface loss) and blood perfusion cooling (λperf = ωb × 63.9 / cp), where ωb [mL/(g·min)] is set in the Advanced panel. In vitro experiments with no blood supply use ωb = 0. The 63.9 factor combines blood density (1060 g/L), specific heat (3617 J/(kg·K)), and unit conversion to s⁻¹ per mL/(g·min). At steady state: Tss = 37 + SAReff / ((λNewton + λperf) × cp).
thermal.scope: Thermal model scope: The Newton cooling coefficient λNewton = 0.02 s⁻¹ (time constant τth ≈ 50 s) represents tissue-level lumped heat dissipation, appropriate for macroscopic electroporation applicators in perfused tissue. A free cell in solution has τth ≈ R²ρcp/κ ≈ 0.6 ms (R = 10 µm, κ ≈ 0.6 W/m·K), equilibrating with its medium in milliseconds. The temperature displayed reflects bulk medium heating, not local membrane temperature, which is relevant for comparing treatment protocols rather than single-pulse effects.
thermal.eqSar: SAR = σ<sub>i</sub> · α² · E² · w<sub>f</sub> / ρ
thermal.eqSarSub1: α = 3σ<sub>e</sub> / (2σ<sub>e</sub> + σ<sub>i</sub>)   (DC internal field factor for sphere in medium)
thermal.eqSarSub2: w<sub>f</sub> = 0.5 (CW sinusoidal)  ∣  1.0 (pulsed bipolar square wave / H-FIRE)
thermal.eqTssSub1: SAR<sub>eff</sub> = SAR<sub>peak</sub> × dc    λ<sub>Newton</sub> = 0.02 s⁻¹ (surface / diffusion cooling)
thermal.eqTssSub2: λ<sub>perf</sub> = ω<sub>b</sub> × 63.9 / c<sub>p</sub>    ω<sub>b</sub> [mL/(g·min)], blood perfusion rate (Advanced panel)
thermal.eqNote: Pennes bioheat equation: Harold H. Pennes, J. Appl. Physiol. 1:93 (1948) [16]  ·  SAR formulation: Kenneth R. Foster & Herman P. Schwan (1989) [5]

maxwell.title: 3.3 Effective Medium (Maxwell-Garnett)
maxwell.tip: Maxwell-Garnett Effective Medium Corrects extracellular conductivity for cell volume fraction φ. σ_eff = σe · (1−φ) / (1+φ/2) (DC insulating-sphere limit) φ = 0: isolated cells · φ ≈ 0.64: random close-packing Applied before computing τ, Vm, and SAR for dense suspensions.
maxwell.p1: At high cell packing densities φ (volume fraction of cells), neighbouring cells reduce the effective extracellular conductivity σe,eff experienced by each cell. This is captured by the Maxwell-Garnett mixing rule [17] for insulating spheres in a conducting medium, the DC limit applicable when cell membranes are capacitive (f ≪ fc). Notably, this formula is mathematically identical to the Hashin-Shtrikman lower bound for insulating inclusions (the tightest rigorous lower bound on σeff), so it is not merely an approximation but the exact lower bound at DC:
maxwell.p2: The simulation applies this correction to σ<sub>e</sub> before computing τ, V<sub>m</sub>, and SAR, so all downstream outputs reflect the dense-suspension environment. φ = 0 corresponds to isolated cells in bulk medium (in vitro single-cell); φ ≈ 0.64-0.74 represents random close-packing of spheres (dense cell aggregate). The Cell Packing slider is in the Advanced panel. For most in vitro well-plate experiments, φ ≈ 0.01-0.05 (sparse); cell aggregates and organoids can reach φ ≈ 0.6-0.8. Note: the Maxwell-Garnett DC formula is the appropriate limit here, the full Bruggeman or Bergman-Milton bounds apply at higher frequencies and are not implemented.
maxwell.eqSub1: φ, cell volume packing fraction (0 = isolated cells; ~0.64 = random close-packing)
maxwell.eqSub2: DC insulating-sphere limit; valid when f ≪ f<sub>c</sub> (membrane capacitively opaque)
maxwell.eqNote: James Clerk Maxwell Garnett, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 203:385 (1904) [17]

disruption.title: 3.4 Disruption Criterion (IRE)
disruption.tip: Disruption Ratio and IRE Criterion DR = Vm(f) × PEF / Vth · PEF = 1−exp(−tp/τ) (RC charging factor) 8-45%: Nourishing: sub-threshold biomodulation active 50-85%: Rev-EP: reversible pores, drug/gene delivery regime >85%: LYSIS ARMED: irreversible EP · lysis countdown starts Fires after N×tp/dc (pulsed) or 2.5 s (CW) H-FIRE: Vth,eff = Vth × 1.75 (bipolar burst, reduced net membrane charging per unit peak field)
disruption.p1: Membrane disruption (irreversible electroporation; Neumann et al. [7]; membrane deformation dynamics reviewed in Dimova et al. [6]) is initiated when the disruption ratio exceeds threshold for a sustained period. The pulse-envelope factor fpulse = 1 − exp(−tp/τ) captures the RC charging dynamics of the membrane during a rectangular pulse of width tp (Weaver & Chizmadzhev [3]): at tp ≫ τ (standard IRE with µs pulses), fpulse ≈ 1 and the listed Vm,threshold values apply directly. At tp ≪ τ (nsEP with 10 ns pulses), fpulse ≈ 0.07 for a hepatocyte, the effective threshold is ~14× higher, requiring proportionally greater field for disruption. CW mode sets fpulse = 1.
disruption.p2: Cancer cells exhibit lower Vm,threshold (~0.65-0.85 V) than healthy tissue (~1.0-1.1 V), creating a selectivity window where tumour cell disruption occurs at sub-lethal field intensities for normal cells. For adenocarcinoma vs. hepatocyte in saline, maximum Vm selectivity ≈ RT/RH = 1.5× occurs at quasi-DC (f ≪ fc(T)); the Selectivity Index (TI) (accounting for different lysis thresholds) reaches ~2.4× at quasi-DC. Selectivity decreases with increasing frequency as the larger target cell rolls off before the smaller healthy cell.
disruption.revEp: The Rev-EP window (50-85% disruption ratio) represents reversible electroporation: pores open transiently and re-seal after the field is removed, the drug/gene delivery regime (cells survive). Displayed as an amber REVERSIBLE EP strip on the target cell card. The Disruption Ratio Chart (↯) shows the frequency range over which this window applies for the current cell pair and field settings, with the rev-EP zone between the amber and red dashed threshold lines. Increasing field or duration beyond 85% transitions to the LYSIS ARMED state and starts the irreversible lysis countdown. The resealing time (shown on the target cell card in Rev-EP state) is estimated as τreseal = τref × (DR/DRref)2.5 × exp(−0.06·(T−37)) × Np0.3, where τref = 5 s at DRref = 0.675 (midpoint of rev-EP window). Higher DR, higher temperature, and more pulses each accelerate permanent damage onset (Rols & Teissie, Biophys. J. 1990); the formula is empirically scaled and clamped to 0.5-60 s.

J. 1999)
disruption.eqSub2: 8-45% → Nourishing: sub-threshold biomodulation window (Ca²⁺ / NO signalling; §2.10); 45-50% → Approaching: membrane stress onset, ion channel perturbation; healthy cells: keep below 50% for selectivity window
disruption.eqSub3: 50-85% → Rev-EP window: reversible electroporation, pores open transiently and re-seal
disruption.eqSub4: Simulation arms lysis countdown when Disruption Ratio > 85% of threshold
disruption.eqSub5: Lysis fires after protocol time: t<sub>lysis</sub> = N × (t<sub>p</sub>/dc) (pulsed) or 2.5 s (CW), where t<sub>p</sub>/dc is the pulse period (full cycle duration), not the pulse width alone
disruption.eqSub6: Structural Integrity Bar (below the LYSIS ARMED strip on the target cell card): drains 100 → 0 % in real time as the lysis countdown elapses, visual confirmation that DR threshold has been held for the full protocol duration
disruption.eqSub7: Disruption Ratio Chart (↯ accordion in Experiment Lab): shows DR(f) across 10 kHz-500 MHz for both cells simultaneously; green-shaded selectivity window where DRT ≥ 85 % and DRH < 50 %; dashed amber = 50 % rev-EP boundary, dashed red = 85 % lysis threshold
disruption.eqSub8: H-FIRE waveform: Bipolar burst pulses at carrier frequency >1 kHz raise the effective lysis threshold by ×1.75 vs. monopolar IRE (Arena et al. [27]; Sano et al. [28]). Polarity reversals partially discharge the membrane capacitance between half-cycles, reducing net Vm per burst. Model: DRH-FIRE = Vm × fpulse / (Vm,threshold × 1.75). Benefit: carrier frequency >1 kHz falls below the neuromuscular activation threshold (~500 Hz), avoiding neurostimulation artefacts in tissue-model experiments.
disruption.hfireNote: H-FIRE (High-Frequency Irreversible Electroporation) delivers bipolar square-wave bursts at intra-burst carrier frequencies of 1-100 kHz. Each polarity reversal partially discharges the membrane capacitance, so the effective transmembrane voltage per burst is reduced relative to monopolar delivery at the same peak field. The practical consequence is a ×1.5-2× higher field requirement to reach the lysis threshold (×1.75 midpoint used in this model, referenced to Sano et al. [28]). The key advantage is that carrier frequencies >1 kHz fall below the neuromuscular activation threshold (~500 Hz), avoiding neurostimulation artefacts in tissue-model and excitable-cell experiments (Arena et al. [27]). Select the H-FIRE waveform pill in the Protocol accordion of the Field Control panel; the Disruption Ratio, SAR, and lysis countdown automatically account for the elevated effective threshold.
disruption.windowScoreNote: Population Window Score (WS), shown in the Selectivity Panel, quantifies protocol selectivity at the whole-population level: WS = P(target lysis) × (1 − P(healthy lysis)), where P denotes the fraction of a randomly-oriented isotropic cell suspension that exceeds the lysis disruption ratio (cosθ orientation model: P = max(0, 1 − 1/DR)). WS near 1.0 indicates near-complete target cell lysis with minimal healthy-cell co-lysis; WS near 0 indicates either the target is sub-threshold or healthy cells are co-lysed. Maximising WS is the primary optimisation objective for selective IRE protocols; use the Population Model panel (∑ accordion) to visualise the underlying radius distributions.
disruption.eqNote: James C. Weaver & Yuri A. Chizmadzhev, Bioelectrochem. Bioenerg. 41:135 (1996) [3]  ·  H-FIRE threshold: Arena et al., Biomed. Eng. Online 10:102 (2011) [27]; Sano et al., Sci. Rep. 5:14999 (2015) [28]

resonance.title: 3.5 Acoustic / Mechanical Resonance, Virus & Bacteria
resonance.tip: Acoustic Resonance Model (Bacteria / Virus) Models mechanical disruption of rigid capsid shells and peptidoglycan walls. Disruption ratio = (E / Ethr) × L(f, fres, Q) L(f) = 1/√(1+(Q·(f/f₀−f₀/f))²) Lorentzian lineshape fres ≈ v_shell/(2R) · Mammalian cells have no rigid-shell resonance.
resonance.p1: For sub-micron targets (virions and bacteria), the Schwan model predicts reduced selectivity at quasi-DC because Vm ∝ R, small cells generate lower transmembrane voltage than large cells. The correct disruption mechanism at GHz frequencies is acoustic/mechanical resonance of the capsid protein shell or bacterial cell wall, modelled by a Lorentzian lineshape. Mammalian cells lack the rigid protein/peptidoglycan shell required for this resonance; their Schwan Vm rolls off above ~1 MHz and approaches zero at GHz frequencies, leaving healthy tissue unperturbed at pathogen-targeting frequencies.
resonance.rfBasis: RF vs. laser excitation: fres values derive from femtosecond pulsed laser (near-IR, ~800 nm) impulsive stimulated Raman scattering experiments (Tsen et al. [10]), not direct RF/microwave delivery. Ethr values for RF excitation are theoretical extrapolations with no experimental validation. The RF-to-GHz-acoustic coupling mechanism is not established in the literature; microwave delivery at 10-12 GHz faces a tissue penetration depth of ~1-2 mm.
resonance.envelopedBasis: Enveloped virus resonance: Tsen [10][11] and Dykeman [12] models were validated on non-enveloped icosahedral protein-capsid viruses (M13, TMV, CCMV). Influenza A (H3N2) and SARS-CoV-2 have since been directly characterised by microwave absorption spectroscopy: Influenza A fres = 8.2 GHz, Q = 2.0 (Thakur et al. Sci. Rep. 2015 [33]); SARS-CoV-2 bimodal absorption at fres1 = 4.0 GHz and fres2 = 7.5 GHz, Q = 4.6 (Sci. Rep. 2022 [34]). Measured Q values indicate moderate, not fully overdamped, damping. Lentivirus fres = 19-21 GHz was measured by ultrafast pump-probe spectroscopy (PNAS 2025 [35]). The primary remaining caveat is Ethr: disruption threshold values are theoretical extrapolations; direct cuvette-coupling validation under RF excitation has not been reported for any enveloped virus.
resonance.bacteriaQ: Bacterial Q-factor: Dykeman [12] models apply to protein capsids, not bacterial cell walls. Peptidoglycan is a viscoelastic polymer mesh with substantially higher damping. Acoustic data for isolated E. coli sacculi suggest Q ≈ 2-5; Q = 4 (E. coli) and Q = 3 (MRSA) are upper estimates. Near Q ≈ 1-2, the concept of a sharp resonance frequency breaks down.
resonance.infoBox: Switch to Resonance mode in the Experiment Lab (mode toggle in the setup bar) when working with bacterial or viral targets. The platform auto-tunes frequency to fres and sets field to 5% of Ethr when a resonance-enabled preset is loaded (a safe sub-threshold starting point; DR ≈ 5% at f_res).

nsep.title: 3.6 Nanosecond Pulsed EP (nsEP), Reference Model
nsep.tip: Nanosecond Pulsed EP: Reference Model Uses DC step response, not AC Schwan model. Vm_eff = 1.5·E·R·cosθ · (1−exp(−tp/τ)) At tp≪τ: small cells (short τ) charge proportionally more than large cells. Lab Pulse Width slider sets lysis timing (PEF), not AC Vm per se.
nsep.p1: Nanosecond pulsed electroporation (nsEP) uses DC rectangular pulses (not sinusoidal RF) applied from specialised pulsed-power generators. The membrane charges as a first-order RC step response: Vm,eff(tp) = 1.5 · E · R · cos θ × (1 − exp(−tp/τ)). At tp = 10 ns in saline: τE.coli ≈ 14 ns → factor ≈ 0.51; τhepatocyte ≈ 147 ns → factor ≈ 0.065. The quasi-DC Vm ratio of 0.10× (E. coli vs. hepatocyte) improves to ~0.78×, the small cell charges proportionally more per pulse than the large cell. The theoretical TI limit as tp → 0 remains below 1× because Vm,thr,bacteria > Vm,thr,hepatocyte (cell-wall reinforcement raises the lysis threshold).
nsep.scope: Simulation scope: The Experiment Lab simulates duty-cycled AC sinusoidal fields, the Schwan Vm(f) model is evaluated at the RF carrier frequency, which is the correct model for continuous-wave RF or pulse-modulated RF bursts. True nsEP (DC rectangular pulses, pulsed-power hardware) uses the step-response formula above. The Pulse Width slider in the lab controls lysis protocol timing and the SAR waveform factor (fpulse), not Vm per se. For dedicated nsEP modelling, use the DC step-response formula directly.
nsep.eqMain: V<sub>m,eff</sub>(t<sub>p</sub>) = 1.5 · E · R · cos θ × (1 − exp(−t<sub>p</sub> / τ))
nsep.eqNote: Michael Stacey et al. [8]; Karl H. Schoenbach, Stephen J. Beebe & Eric S. Buescher [13]

doubleshell.title: 3.7 Double-Shell Nuclear Envelope Model
doubleshell.tip: Double-Shell Nuclear Envelope (Kotnik 2006) Adds nuclear membrane as a second concentric dielectric shell. Nuclear Vm is a bandpass function, peaking at fpeak = 1/(2π√(τ_out·τ_ne)) For presets: fpeak ≈ 0.74-1.66 MHz (±30% model accuracy vs full Kotnik 2006) Enable via Shell Model toggle in Field Control. Schwan mode only.
doubleshell.p1: For mammalian nucleated cells, an optional double-shell model (Kotnik & Miklavcic 2006 [15]) adds the nuclear membrane as a second concentric dielectric shell. The nuclear membrane Vm is a two-pole bandpass function of frequency, with peak at fpeak = 1/(2π√(τout·τne)), typically in the 0.74-1.66 MHz range for the presets in this library. Cancer cells have a higher nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N/C) ratio, thinner nuclear envelopes, and lower nuclear Vm thresholds, creating an additional cancer-selectivity axis. Enable via the Shell Model toggle in the Field Control panel.
doubleshell.fpeak: fpeak model accuracy: The formula fpeak = 1/(2π√(τout·τne)) is exact for the simplified nuclear Vm expression used here (proven by setting d/dω of the bandpass numerator to zero). The ±30% caveat applies at the model level: the simplified two-time-constant formula deviates from the full Kotnik & Miklavcic (2006) two-shell transfer function by up to ±30% when 0.1 < τout/τne < 10, which includes all presets in this library. Displayed fpeak values are exact for the implemented model; use the full two-pole transfer function (Kotnik & Miklavcic 2006, Eq. 12) for higher-accuracy estimates.
doubleshell.thinShell: Thin-shell approximation: The model assumes Rnuc ≪ R (dilute-nucleus limit). For the adenocarcinoma preset, Rnuc/R = 8/15 ≈ 0.53, near the boundary of validity. At this N/C ratio, the sphere-in-infinite-medium assumption underestimates nuclear field concentration by ~15%. The model remains a useful qualitative predictor of bandpass frequency and cancer selectivity trends.
doubleshell.sigmaNote: σ<sub>ne</sub> is not stored or used in the simulation. The implementation operates in the thin-membrane capacitive limit (σ<sub>ne</sub> → 0), per Kotnik & Miklavcic (2006) Eq. (14). Including finite σ<sub>ne</sub> requires the full complex admittance transfer function and is left for future work.
doubleshell.eqMain: V<sub>m,nuc</sub>(f) = (1.5 · E · R<sub>nuc</sub> · cos θ · ω·τ<sub>out</sub>) / √[(1+(ωτ<sub>out</sub>)²) · (1+(ωτ<sub>ne</sub>)²)]
doubleshell.eqNote: Tadej Kotnik & Damijan Miklavcic, Biophys. J. 90:480 (2006) [15]

dep.title: 3.8 Dielectrophoresis (DEP)
dep.tip: Dielectrophoresis: Clausius-Mossotti Factor Re[K(f)] ∈ [-0.5, +0.5]: determines DEP force direction. Re[K] > 0: pDEP, attracted to field maxima (electrode edges) Re[K] < 0: nDEP, repelled from field maxima F_DEP = 2π·εm·R³·Re[K]·∇|E|² · Model invalid at GHz resonance frequencies.
dep.p1: Dielectrophoresis (DEP) is the translational motion of a polarisable particle placed in a spatially non-uniform electric field. Unlike electrophoresis (which requires a net charge), DEP arises from the induced dipole generated by the mismatch between particle and medium permittivity, and operates on all cells regardless of charge. The time-averaged DEP force on a spherical cell of radius R is:
dep.eqForceSub: ε<sub>m</sub> = ε<sub>r,medium</sub> · ε₀, permittivity of the suspension medium
dep.p2: The sign of the Clausius-Mossotti (CM) factor Re[K(ω)] ∈ [−0.5, +0.5] determines the force direction. Re[K] > 0: positive DEP (pDEP), the cell is attracted to field maxima (electrode edges, channel constrictions). Re[K] < 0: negative DEP (nDEP), the cell is repelled from field maxima. The crossover frequency fcross is where Re[K] = 0 and the polarity reverses.
dep.eqCmSub1: ε*(ω) = ε<sub>r</sub> · ε₀ − j σ/ω, complex permittivity
dep.eqCmSub3: γ = ((R − d) / R)³, volume ratio factor (d = membrane thickness)
dep.eqNote: Gascoyne & Vykoukal, Electrophoresis 23:1973 (2002); Pethig R., Biomicrofluidics 4:022811 (2010)
dep.p3: At low frequencies (f ≪ f<sub>c</sub>), the membrane is capacitively opaque and the cell behaves as an insulating sphere: Re[K] → −0.5 regardless of σ<sub>cyto</sub> (nDEP, cell repelled from field maxima). Above f<sub>c</sub>, current penetrates the membrane and Re[K] is set by the conductivity contrast. For mammalian cells in physiological saline (σ<sub>cyto</sub> ≈ 0.5-0.9 S/m, σ<sub>saline</sub> ≈ 1.5 S/m): σ<sub>cyto</sub> < σ<sub>medium</sub> → Re[K] remains negative (nDEP). In low-conductivity EP buffer (σ<sub>e</sub> ≈ 0.14 S/m): σ<sub>cyto</sub> > σ<sub>medium</sub> → Re[K] becomes positive (pDEP) above f<sub>c</sub>, then a crossover to nDEP occurs at high frequency where permittivity dominates. At high frequencies, ε<sub>r,cyto</sub> ≈ 60 falls below ε<sub>r,medium</sub> ≈ 78-80, giving nDEP. The crossover frequency depends on cell size, membrane capacitance, and medium conductivity; use EP buffer to observe the pDEP regime for mammalian cells.
dep.p4: Waveform and duty cycle: The Clausius-Mossotti factor Re[K(f)] is a material property of the cell-medium system and is independent of waveform. However, the time-averaged DEP force depends on the waveform envelope. For CW sinusoidal fields, the time-average gives a factor of ½. For pulsed waveforms (H-FIRE protocol), the time-averaged force scales with the duty cycle dc. The chart always shows raw Re[K](f); the waveform scale factor (×0.50 for CW, ×dc for pulsed) is shown separately in the Selectivity Panel DEP row.
dep.warnBox: Model validity: The single-shell sphere DEP model is applicable in the kHz to hundreds of MHz range. It is not valid at GHz acoustic resonance frequencies (bacteria/virus resonance mode); in that regime, the acoustic mechanical model applies and the CM factor calculation should not be used. E. coli is rod-shaped; the sphere approximation gives qualitatively correct crossover frequency but not precise force magnitudes. Virion Schwan fc is highly σi-dependent: for protein-dense capsid interiors (σi,eff ≈ 10⁻⁴-10⁻³ S/m, protein crystal range), τ ≈ R·Cm/σi is large and fc can be sub-kHz (ωτ ≫ 1 at all practical lab frequencies); for nucleic-acid-filled interiors with higher effective σi (0.01-0.1 S/m), fc shifts into the 100 kHz-10 MHz range. The ±45% σi uncertainty (§2.9) makes this range highly uncertain for any specific virion. DEP crossover for viruses may lie outside the typical operating window or may not exist at accessible frequencies.

uncertainty.title: 3.9 Cytoplasm Conductivity (σ<sub>i</sub>) Uncertainty
uncertainty.tip: σi Uncertainty Bands σi controls τ, SAR, Vm, and TI simultaneously (highest-impact uncertain parameter). Uncertainty: ±20% mammalian · ±35% bacteria · ±45% virus Shown as shaded bands on the Bode chart (cyan: healthy, red: target). TI uncertainty range in Selectivity Panel applies worst-case σi bounds.
uncertainty.p1: Cytoplasm conductivity σ<sub>i</sub> is the most influential uncertain parameter in the Schwan model: it controls both τ and the SAR internal field factor α, affecting V<sub>m</sub>, f<sub>c</sub>, temperature, and the Selectivity Index (TI) simultaneously. Literature values span considerable ranges depending on measurement technique (impedance spectroscopy, patch-clamp, rotation assay), ionic composition, growth phase, and osmolarity.
uncertainty.p2: The simulation visualises σi uncertainty as shaded bands on the frequency response chart (healthy: cyan, target: red, 10% opacity each). The band bounds are ±20% for mammalian cells, ±35% for bacteria, and ±45% for viruses. The TI uncertainty range displayed in the Selectivity Panel computes worst-case Selectivity Index (TI) bounds: TIlow applies maximum σi penalty for the target and minimum for healthy; TIhigh applies the inverse. These bounds represent the realistic spread of outcomes across the literature parameter ranges, not measurement error or model uncertainty per se.

biomodulation.title: 3.10 Sub-threshold Biomodulation (Empirical Index)
biomodulation.tip: Sub-threshold Biomodulation (Empirical Index) Automatic state, no mode toggle. Active when healthy cell DR 8-45%. Pathways: PIEZO1 Ca²⁺ influx + CaM-NOS nitric oxide (Pilla 2012; Lee 2018) BMS = 0.55·SI + 0.25·MTE + 0.20·MA IMPORTANT: The BMS formula, weighting coefficients, and MTE definition are exploratory constructs with no peer-reviewed validation. Use for qualitative exploration only. Not a clinical or research-grade index. Optimal parameters: pulsed mode, dc ≈ 10⁻⁴, f < fc, DR ≈ 20-40%.
biomodulation.empiricalWarn: Empirical Index Warning: The Biomodulation Score (BMS) and its components (SI, MTE, MA) are simulator constructs with no peer-reviewed validation for the specific formula, weight coefficients, or MTE definition. The MTE term reuses the Schwan electrical roll-off as a proxy for mechanical coupling, which conflates two distinct physical mechanisms. The underlying Ca²⁺ and NO signalling pathways are experimentally established; the composite BMS scoring is not. Treat this section as a qualitative exploration tool, not a quantitative research output.
biomodulation.p1: At DR 8-45%, pulsed fields activate mechanosensitive and voltage-gated ion channels without causing lysis. The simulation labels this the Nourishing state (8-45% DR, below the NOURISHING = 45% threshold): a simulator convention for the sub-lytic biomodulation window, not a clinical category. Two established in vitro pathways drive the response:
biomodulation.eqMain: BMS = 0.55 · SI + 0.25 · MTE + 0.20 · MA  (empirical, coefficients not peer-reviewed)
biomodulation.eqSub1: SI = Stimulation Index (sub-threshold V<sub>m</sub> / nourishing threshold)  ·  active at DR 20-40%
biomodulation.eqSub2: MTE = Electrical coupling factor (Schwan roll-off proxy; not a validated mechanical transduction model)  ·  MA = Mild Thermal Activation (T 37-41°C window)
biomodulation.eqNote: Pilla A.A., Biochem. Biophys. Res. Commun. 426:330 (2012) [18]  ·  Pall M.L., J. Cell Mol. Med. 17:958 (2013) [19]  ·  BMS formula: simulator construct, not from cited works
biomodulation.p2: (1) PIEZO1 / voltage-gated Ca²⁺: Sub-threshold fields generate transient intracellular Ca²⁺ spikes at DR 20-40% via two distinct pathways: PIEZO1 mechanosensitive channels (stretch-activated, gated indirectly by field-induced membrane tension and deformation rather than by the field potential directly) and VGCCs (voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, directly activated by the sub-threshold transmembrane potential), without permanent permeabilisation. Ca²⁺ drives downstream gene expression and cytoskeletal remodelling (Pall [19]). (2) CaM-NOS nitric oxide: Ca²⁺ influx activates calmodulin-dependent NOS, modulating NO production with reported effects on vasodilation and inflammation resolution (Pilla [18]). In vitro evidence is well-established; translation to in vivo outcomes remains an active research area and is not modelled here. Recommended parameters: pulsed mode, dc ≈ 10⁻⁵-10⁻⁴, f < fc, DR ≈ 20-40%.

impedance.title: 3.11 Impedance Feedback & Ion Release Model
impedance.tip: Impedance Feedback and Ion Release Lysed cells release cytoplasm, shifting σe by φ·flysed·(σi−σe₀)·η. Direction: σe rises (Z drops) when σi > σe₀ (low-σ EP buffer). σe falls (Z rises) when σi < σe₀ (saline/PBS with mammalian cells). Voltage divider: Efield = Egen × Z/(Z+Rs). Corrected: Egen = Etarget × (1+Rs/Z). Instrument Panel tracks drift; connect hardware via impedanceReading socket event.
impedance.p1: As cells lyse during an electroporation protocol, intracellular ions (K⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻, ATP, and other solutes) are released into the extracellular medium. This ion release shifts the medium conductivity σ<sub>e</sub> according to σ<sub>e</sub>(t) = σ<sub>e₀</sub> + φ·f<sub>lysed</sub>·(σ<sub>i</sub>−σ<sub>e₀</sub>)·η. The direction depends on the conductivity contrast: in low-conductivity EP buffers (σ<sub>e₀</sub> ≈ 0.1 S/m, σ<sub>i</sub> ≈ 0.5-0.7 S/m), lysis raises σ<sub>e</sub> and lowers the cuvette impedance Z = d/(σ<sub>e</sub>·A). In high-conductivity media such as saline or PBS (σ<sub>e₀</sub> = 1.5 S/m, σ<sub>i</sub> ≈ 0.5-0.7 S/m for mammalian cells), σ<sub>i</sub> < σ<sub>e₀</sub> so lysis slightly reduces σ<sub>e</sub> and raises Z instead; at typical cell densities of 10<sup>6</sup> cells/mL the effect is negligible (<0.1%). The impedance drift problem is most significant in EP buffer at high cell concentrations. In either case, the generator and cable have a source impedance R<sub>s</sub> (typically 50 Ω), forming a voltage divider with the cuvette. Without field correction, the delivered field deviates from the set point (Kotnik et al. [22]).
impedance.p2: The Instrument Panel (/instrument) models this drift in real time. The ion-release model computes the live conductivity from the current disruption ratio; the corrected generator output is then displayed so the operator knows exactly how much to increase the generator voltage to maintain a constant intra-cuvette field.
impedance.eqMain: σ<sub>e</sub>(t) = σ<sub>e₀</sub> + φ · f<sub>lysed</sub> · (σ<sub>i</sub> − σ<sub>e₀</sub>) · η
impedance.eqSub1: φ = N · (4/3)π R³  ·  cell volume fraction
impedance.eqSub2: f<sub>lysed</sub> = max(0, (DR − 0.85) / 0.15)  ·  fraction of cells past lysis threshold
impedance.eqSub3: η = 0.8  ·  ion-release efficiency (reduced by protein-polymer crowding in released cytoplasm)
impedance.eqZ: Z = d / (σ<sub>e</sub> · A)  ·  DC cuvette impedance [Ω]  ·  valid for f ≪ 340 MHz in saline
impedance.eqCorr: E<sub>gen</sub> = E<sub>target</sub> × (1 + R<sub>s</sub> / Z)  ·  corrected generator field [V/cm]
impedance.eqNote: Kotnik, Rems, Tarek & Miklavcic, Annu. Rev. Biophys. 48:63 (2019) [22]; cuvette DC model: standard electrochemistry
impedance.hardwareP: In the default Simulated mode the ion-release model drives the impedance display. To replace the simulation with real instrument data, connect an impedance analyser or LCR meter to the ResoPulse backend socket and emit the impedanceReading event. The backend validates the packet and re-broadcasts impedanceBroadcast to all connected UI clients. Switch the Sensor Mode toggle to Live Hardware in the Hardware Input card to activate this override. The hardware Zreal replaces the simulated value; σe is back-derived as σ = d/(Zreal·A).

sonification.title: 3.12 Auditory Display (Sonification)
sonification.tip: Auditory Display (Sonification) Maps live physics values to sound via Web Audio API. Impedance drift → pitch (220-1760 Hz) · DR → volume Rev-EP state → 6 Hz tremolo · Lysis event → 880 Hz burst IMPORTANT: These are data representations, NOT the RF applied-field frequencies.
sonification.p1: Sonification is the use of non-speech audio to convey information. In the context of this platform, live experiment parameters are mapped to audible tones via the Web Audio API, enabling an operator to monitor experiment state without continuously watching the screen, a technique first formalised by Kramer et al. (1999) [23]. The technique is particularly suited to multi-parameter monitoring during long electroporation protocols where both impedance drift and cell disruption ratio evolve simultaneously.
sonification.disclaimer: Important: These sounds are NOT the RF applied-field frequencies. The electroporation and resonance frequencies used in this platform are in the kHz-GHz range, far above the 20 Hz-20 kHz audible spectrum. The sonification maps data values to audible tones; it has no physical relationship to the applied field and does not affect the cells.

mappings.note: Higher drift = higher pitch; maps absolute drift % linearly to frequency
Louder = higher DR; scales from 0% to 100% lysis
Amplitude modulation flags the reversible electroporation window
Single A5 tone marks the lysis threshold crossing
Warning: healthy cell has entered the critical co-lysis risk zone

sonification.p2: The Auditory Display is enabled from the Instrument Panel via the ♪ button. The pitch bar below the button shows the current pitch frequency in real time. All mappings follow the design principles in Walker & Kramer (2005) [24]: pitch is an effective ordinal scale for scalar quantities; AM tremolo is a distinctive qualitative marker for state transitions; and the mapping direction (higher = more disrupted) is intuitive and consistent with spectral urgency conventions.
sonification.refNote: Kramer G. et al., Sonification Report: Status of the Field and Research Agenda. ICAD (1999) [23]  ·  Walker B.N. & Kramer G., Mappings and Metaphors in Auditory Displays. ACM Trans. Appl. Percept. 2005 [24]

electrosensitization.title: 3.13 Multi-Pulse Electrosensitization (N-Pulse Threshold Reduction)
electrosensitization.tip: Electrosensitization Model V_th_eff = V_th × N^(−0.20) × temp_correction Empirical population-averaged model; exponent varies by cell type. Acoustic resonance thresholds are not affected.
electrosensitization.p1: When a cell suspension is subjected to repeated above-threshold pulses, each pulse creates a population of membrane pores that partially persist until the next pulse arrives. This pre-conditioning lowers the effective lysis threshold for subsequent pulses, a phenomenon termed electrosensitization or cumulative membrane conditioning (Weaver & Chizmadzhev 1996 [3]; Pakhomov et al. 2010 [25]). The simulation models this as a multiplicative reduction of the nominal lysis threshold voltage Vth:
electrosensitization.eqSub2: N = pulse count (Pulse Count slider); N = 1 → no reduction (single-pulse baseline)
electrosensitization.eqSub3: f<sub>temp</sub>(T) = max(0.70, 1 − 0.003 × (T − 37°C)), temperature correction factor (0.3%/°C above 37°C, capped at 30% max reduction; Weaver & Chizmadzhev [3])
electrosensitization.eqSub4: Floor: N<sup>−0.20</sup> is clamped to a minimum of 0.35 (35% of nominal threshold), preventing unphysical sub-physiological values at very large N
electrosensitization.eqSub5: Acoustic resonance thresholds (resonantThresholdVcm) are NOT modified by N. Mechanical capsid disruption has no pulse-conditioning equivalent, it is a physical resonance phenomenon, not a pore-formation process.

examples.note: Moderate reduction; typical IRE burst protocol range
Standard multi-pulse EP; threshold 37% below nominal
Near clamp floor; diminishing returns above N ~ 80
Clamped to floor, model no longer predicts further reduction

electrosensitization.warnBox: Model limitations and honesty statement: The N−0.20 formula is a population-averaged empirical approximation derived from bulk electroporation dose-response literature. It should be understood as a first-order protocol design tool, not a cell-specific quantitative prediction. The following limitations apply: (1) Exponent α is cell-type dependent. Cells with thin, fluid membranes (e.g. erythrocytes, small bacteria with thin peptidoglycan) sensitize faster (α closer to 0.3-0.4); cells with reinforced membranes (MRSA, thick-wall gram-positives) sensitize more slowly (α closer to 0.1-0.15). The fixed α = 0.20 is the midpoint of the published range. (2) Pulse interval matters. If inter-pulse interval is long enough for membrane resealing, electrosensitization is reduced or eliminated. This model assumes pulses arrive within the resealing window (typically sub-second for IRE pulse trains). (3) The clamp at 35% is a conservative physiological floor, not a measured value. At very high N, the true threshold asymptote depends on cell-type-specific pore-size distributions and lipid composition. (4) This model is not validated for acoustic resonance. The N slider has no effect on resonant disruption thresholds, which are mechanical properties of the capsid or cell wall. See §3.5 for the acoustic model.
electrosensitization.refNote: Weaver J.C. & Chizmadzhev Y.A., Theory of electroporation: a review. Bioelectrochemistry and Bioenergetics 41:135 (1996) [3]  ·  Pakhomov A.G. et al., Long-lasting plasma membrane permeabilization in mammalian cells by nanosecond pulsed electric field (nsPEF). Bioelectromagnetics 28:655 (2007) [25]  ·  Rols M.P. & Teissié J., Electropermeabilization of mammalian cells: quantitative analysis of the phenomenon. Biophys. J. 58:1089 (1990)

s01.title: Select cell pair
s01.desc: In the Experiment Lab, use the preset picker in the setup bar to choose healthy reference and target cell types. Built-in library presets load peer-reviewed biophysical parameters from the cell library (see Data Sets tab). To use your own measured parameters, click + New Target Cell or + New Reference Cell directly in the picker: the new profile is saved to your shared lab library and appears alongside built-in presets in every session. Open the Cell Parameters panel on either card to enter custom values or perform sensitivity analysis. For bacteria and virus targets, the mode toggle automatically offers Resonance mode.

s02.title: Set propagation medium
s02.desc: Choose the extracellular medium using the Medium dropdown in the Field Control panel (Saline, Blood, Tissue, DMEM, PBS, RPMI, MHB, EP Buffer, or Water). Medium conductivity σe directly modifies τ for all cells, shifting fc markers on the chart and scaling Vm. Physiological saline (σe = 1.5 S/m) is the standard reference for in vitro experiments; DMEM (σe = 1.4 S/m) for cell culture; PBS pH 7.4 (σe = 1.54 S/m) for standard biochemistry buffers. EP Buffer (σe = 0.14 S/m, low-conductivity sucrose/glucose-based) is the electroporation-optimised choice: the lower σe substantially lengthens τ, lowers fc, and shifts mammalian cells from nDEP to pDEP above fc, the preferred medium for selective IRE protocols. To model cells in a tissue-mimicking conductivity environment, select Tissue (σe = 0.4 S/m) and enable blood perfusion via the Advanced panel. The live conductivity readout (σ_e) is shown in the medium row.

s03.title: Configure advanced parameters
s03.desc: Open the Advanced accordion in the Field Control panel to set: Cell Orientation θ (default 60°, the mean |cos θ| = 0.5 for an isotropic 3D suspension; set to 0° only for DEP-aligned cells; orientation scales Vm equally for both cells so it cancels in the selectivity ratio); Blood Perfusion ωb (0 for in vitro; 0.5-5 mL/(g·min) for tissue; adds Pennes cooling term); Cell Packing φ (0 for isolated cells; up to 0.74 for dense tissue; applies Maxwell-Garnett σe correction). All values update τ, Vm, SAR, and Tss in real time.

s04.title: Establish baseline at sub-threshold field
s04.desc: Begin with the default field intensity (10 V/cm for mammalian cancer targets; resonance presets start at 5% of E_thr). Both cells should display disruption ratios well below 8% (Stable state). Use the Protocol snap presets (Quasi-DC, Selective, nsEP, Thermal) at the top of the Protocol section for quick starting configurations. Click Log Reading in the Experiment Log panel to record the baseline state. This first manual entry anchors the session dataset.

s05.title: Identify the optimal frequency window
s05.desc: Cancer / IRE mode: Selectivity is maximised at quasi-DC (f ≪ fc(T), Vm ratio = RT/RH). Click ⭐ in the Selectivity Panel to snap to the computed optimal. Expand the Selectivity Window Planner heatmap (below the Selectivity Panel) to survey TI across the full frequency × field space; click any cell to navigate there directly. Bacteria / virus (Resonance mode): Switch mode via the toggle in the setup bar; the platform auto-tunes to fres and sets field to 5% of Ethr.

s06.title: Increase field intensity toward target threshold
s06.desc: Raise Field Intensity incrementally; monitor disruption ratios on both cell cards and the Selectivity Panel bars. For adenocarcinoma vs. hepatocyte in saline at quasi-DC, lysis threshold crosses near ~622 V/cm (at the default θ=60° orientation; ~311 V/cm at θ=0°) while healthy DR stays below 50%. Expand the ↯ Disruption Ratio Chart to verify the current frequency sits within the green selectivity window (DRT ≥ 85%, DRH < 50%) and assess frequency bandwidth. Use the Field Sweep panel to scan DR vs. field; when a window exists the ⭐ Set to Window Center bar appears below the Selectivity Panel. Log readings at each threshold crossing.

s07.title: Record lysis event and review temperature
s07.desc: When DR > 85%, the red LYSIS ARMED strip appears on the target cell card and the Structural Integrity Bar begins draining from 100 % → 0 % over the protocol time (tlysis = N × tp/dc for pulsed, or 2.5 s for CW). When it reaches 0 %, lysis fires and an entry is automatically added to the Experiment Log with event type lysis. Check the temperature readout on both cell cards. If temperature approaches 42 °C, consider: (a) reducing field intensity, (b) increasing blood perfusion ωb, (c) switching to a lower-conductivity medium to reduce SAR, or (d) switching to the H-FIRE waveform (×1.75 threshold, requires proportionally higher field but allows lower duty cycle for same effect, reducing SAReff). For nsEP targeting, reduce duty cycle, SAReff = SARpeak × dc.

s08.title: Explore biomodulation window (optional)
s08.desc: For research into sub-threshold biomodulation, reduce field to achieve DR ≈ 20-40% of threshold (Nourishing state). This range activates PIEZO1 and voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels without causing lysis. Use pulsed mode with low duty cycle (dc ≈ 10⁻⁴). Log readings to document the sub-threshold state in the session CSV.

s09.title: Change cell preset and repeat parametric study
s09.desc: Switch to a different target preset (e.g. GBM, MCF-7, E. coli) and repeat steps 4-7. Compare selectivity ratios, fc positions, and lysis thresholds across cell types. Use the Cell Parameters panel and σi uncertainty bands on the chart to assess sensitivity to parameter variability. Cell Population Model: Open the Population Model panel and set a radius variance (1-30%) to model a log-normal cell size distribution (CV = variance/mean). The lysis fraction is computed by midpoint rectangle-rule quadrature over 60 z-intervals spanning ±4.5σ of the log-normal distribution (covering >99.999% of mass). The histogram shows the distribution of disruption ratios and the fraction of cells in each state (Lysed %, Rev-EP %, Nourishing %). This quantifies protocol efficacy across biological heterogeneity, critical for assessing whether all target cells are reached by a given protocol while healthy cells remain sub-threshold.

s10.title: Export session data for analysis
s10.desc: Navigate to the Reports tab to review the full session log. Edit the session name, then click Export CSV to download a structured file containing all logged parameters: frequency, field, Vm, selectivity ratio, disruption ratios, temperatures, and event type.

s11.title: Monitor and compensate impedance drift (Instrument Panel)
s11.desc: Navigate to the Instrument tab. Verify the Cuvette Setup card matches your cuvette geometry (gap, cross-section, source impedance Rs). The Live Impedance card shows simulated σe rise as cells lyse; the Field Correction card shows the corrected generator voltage to maintain constant delivered field. A 1 mm BTX cuvette (A = 0.10 cm²) with saline (σe = 1.5 S/m) starts at Z = d/(σe·A) ≈ 67 Ω. In high-conductivity media (PBS, saline), mammalian cells have σi < σe, so lysis releases lower-conductivity cytoplasm into the medium, slightly raising Z (field rises; no corrective increase needed at typical cell densities of 106 cells/mL). The significant impedance-drop scenario occurs in low-conductivity EP buffers (σe ≈ 0.1 S/m, σi ≈ 0.5-0.7 S/m): here σe rises as cells lyse, Z drops, and the delivered field falls; a generator voltage increase of 10-30% may be required at high cell densities (Kotnik et al. 2019 [22]). The Field Correction card in the Instrument panel displays the corrected generator output for whichever direction the drift runs. For live hardware, connect via the instrument bridge (instrument-bridge run --driver <name>) using any supported driver: demo (synthetic, no hardware), ascii_serial (DE-5000/BK Precision via RS-232), btx (BTX ECM 830/2001), visa_lcr (Keysight E4980A, Hioki IM3533/3536), nanopulse (Pulse Biosciences NanoPulse), or pulse_select (Pulse Biosciences PulseSelect). Switch the Sensor Mode toggle to Live Hardware to activate. See §2.11 for socket schema and driver configuration details.

s12.title: Enable auditory display for hands-free monitoring
s12.desc: On the Instrument Panel, click ♪ Auditory Display. Impedance drift maps to pitch (220-1760 Hz); DR controls gain; Rev-EP state triggers 6 Hz AM tremolo; lysis event produces an 880 Hz burst. These tones are data representations only, NOT the RF applied-field frequencies used in the experiment. Browser audio permission required. See §2.12 for full mapping table and references.
